items.text: VTubers are online entertainers who use animated characters, controlled through motion capture , instead of showing their real faces. They sing, play games, and interact live on platforms like Twitch and YouTube, often keeping their real identities private. In Birmingham, the first night of Vexo, short for VTuber Expo, brought together thousands of fans eager to see their favorite VTubers perform. For many fans, the event felt like a concert, but with a digital twist . Meet-and-greet booths allowed fans to interact one-on-one with their favorite creators. VTubers have long been popular in Asia, with concerts in Japan attracting tens of thousands of people. Now, the trend is spreading quickly in the West. During the lockdown in 2020, many young people discovered VTubers on TikTok and YouTube, fueling growth. Vexo’s ticket sales and attendance more than doubled compared to last year, showing increasing popularity. Platforms like Twitch confirm that UK audiences now spend three times more hours watching VTuber streams than a year ago. Difficult words: motion capture (a technology that records the movements of a person to a computer, so that it can copy them for a digital character), twist (a new or different way of doing something), booth (a small space or room at an event where people can meet, see, or buy things). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

Birmingham, UK, hosted Vexo, a big event for VTubers, short for Virtual YouTubers. These are real people who use special technology to control animated characters. They perform music, play games, or chat with fans on websites like Twitch and YouTube. At the Expo, fans could also meet their favorite VTubers in special booths . For many people, it felt like a music concert, but with a digital style. VTubers are already very popular in Japan, where thousands of people go to concerts. In the UK, they are getting more attention . Many fans first found VTubers during the 2020 lockdown. This year’s Vexo attracted more than twice as many visitors as last year, and streaming numbers show that UK fans now watch three times more VTuber content than before. Difficult words: animated (a character or picture which moves like a cartoon and is not real), booth (a small space or room at an event where people can meet, see, or buy things), attention (looking at or listening to something carefully). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

In Birmingham, UK, many people go to Vexo, a show for VTubers. A VTuber is a person who uses a cartoon character instead of showing their face. They sing, play games, and talk to fans online. At the Expo, fans see VTubers on stage and also met them in small rooms. It is like a music concert, but different. VTubers are very popular in Japan, and now they are growing in the UK too. Many young people find VTubers in 2020 when they stay home during lockdown. This year, more than double the people come to Vexo compared to last year. Fans in the UK also watch three times more VTuber videos online now than before. Difficult words: cartoon (a drawing which looks like a person or animal), stage (the place where people perform), double (two times more). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Researchers performed an experiment on the Helags Glacier in northern Sweden. They used a cloth sheet to shield a part of the glacier over the summer, and they said that the cloth saved at least 3.5 meters in height from melting. The sheet was about one and a half meters thick, and it was very strong and durable. It hindered the sun and UV radiation, and it also isolated the ice from warm air. Global warming is causing glaciers to shrink all over the world, and researchers hope to redo their test on a larger size, so they can raise awareness about the dangers many people will face if the glaciers disappear. Difficult words: shield (to protect from danger or risk), hinder (to block or put something in the way), shrink (to be or make smaller). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

Swedish scientists did an experiment on the Helags Glacier in the north of the country. The scientists put a special cloth on the top of the glacier during the summer months. The cloth was made of very strong and durable material which blocked the sun and UV radiation . It also kept the glacier cold. The team said that they saved at least 3.5 meters of ice from melting . Glaciers are melting all over the world as a result of warmer temperatures. It is important that more people know about the problem because it will be more serious in the future, and people will have to solve it. Difficult words: durable (something that lasts for a long time without any damage), UV radiation (some of the energy which comes from the sun), melt (to become soft or change into water). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Swedish scientists do an experiment . They put a cloth on a glacier . The glacier is the Helags Glacier in the north of Sweden. All glaciers in the world are melting . This happens because the planet is getting warmer. Scientists are thinking of ways on how to stop it. They put a cloth on the top of the Helags Glacier in summer. The cloth stops the sun. It keeps the glacier cold. Scientists save at least 3.5 meters of ice. The ice does not melt. The melting of glaciers is a serious problem. Scientists believe that more people know about the problem now. Difficult words: experiment (a test which scientists do to learn something or find if something is true), glacier (a river of ice), melt (to change from ice or snow to water). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

In recent years, Asia has seen an escalation of protests, from Sri Lanka’s economic crisis to Bangladesh’s political collapse, as well as violent uprisings in Nepal and Indonesia. Social media has played a central role in these events, helping young activists to mobilize and demand change. Platforms like TikTok, Instagram, and Discord allowed fast communication and coordination, but they also became breeding grounds for misinformation. In Nepal, misleading posts such as rumours of a military coup or attacks on temples fueled violence. Viral content like “NepoBabies” videos showing politicians’ children living in luxury heightened public anger against corruption. In some cases, misinformation directly incited attacks, such as when a widely circulated map of politicians’ homes led to arson, leaving even family members injured. Analysts warn that although social media empowers citizens, it can also destabilize movements. With elections approaching, some fear organized groups may weaponize misinformation more deliberately in the future. Difficult words: mobilize (to bring people together to take action), breeding ground (a place or situation where something grows easily), incite (to make people act angrily or violently). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

Across Asia, protests grow, bring down governments in Sri Lanka and Bangladesh, and people fill the streets in Nepal and Indonesia. Young people often use social media to plan and share ideas. Platforms like TikTok and Discord helped them connect quickly, but they also spread false stories. In Nepal, videos showed children of politicians enjoying luxury while many young people couldn’t find work. Anger grew, and misinformation spread rumours about temple attacks. A map of politicians’ homes led some people to burn houses, which caused injuries. Experts say social media can be powerful, but it is also dangerous. With new elections coming, they worry that false information will grow even stronger. Difficult words: luxury (something very expensive and not necessary), misinformation (wrong or false information that people share), rumour (information that may not be true, passed from person to person). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

In Asia, many people join protests. In Sri Lanka and Bangladesh, leaders lose power. In Nepal and Indonesia, there are fights in the street. Young people use social media like TikTok to talk and make plans. Young people want a better future . Social media is fast, but it also gives false stories. In Nepal, videos show the rich children of politicians having holidays. Poor young people get angry. Some false posts say that the army takes power or that a temple is in danger. A map shows where politicians live, and some houses burn. People worry that this can happen again. With elections soon, false news can cause more problems. Difficult words: future (the time that will come), poor (not having enough money or things to live well), election (when people vote for new leaders). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Boncuk, a devoted pet, spent days waiting outside a hospital in Trabzon, Turkey, where her sick owner, Cemal Senturk, was being treated. According to local media, the dog followed the ambulance that transported Senturk to hospital and she made multiple visits to the front door. Senturk’s daughter said that the dog had been waiting at the hospital for several days, and when she took Boncuk home, the dog kept going back. After six days, Boncuk and her owner were reunited when he was discharged from hospital. Senturk confirmed that his dog was very used to him and that he missed her constantly, too. He said that dogs provided companionship just like humans, they brought joy and made people happy. Difficult words: devoted (very loving or loyal), discharged (officially released or allowed to leave), companionship (spending time with someone you know and like to be with). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

A Turkish man named Cemal Senturk has a dog called Boncuk. Senturk and Boncuk have a very strong relationship , and they are used to being together all the time. Recently, Senturk had to go to hospital and an ambulance took him there. Boncuk followed the ambulance and stayed outside the hospital. The dog waited there for a few days, and Senturk’s daughter took her home. Then, the dog ran back to the hospital and she did it several times. After six days, doctors released Senturk from the hospital and he and his dog finally met again. It was a very happy moment for both of them. Senturk said that he missed his dog very much. He said that dogs make people happy and they could be their best friends. Difficult words: relationship (a situation in which usually two people spent time together or they have feelings for each other), used to (when something is usual or normal for somebody), release (to let go). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Cemal Senturk comes from Turkey. He has a dog. His dog’s name is Boncuk. Senturk and Boncuk are best friends. Senturk must go to hospital. An ambulance takes him there. His dog runs after the ambulance. She waits in front of the hospital. She sits there for three days. Senturk’s daughter takes the dog home. The dog returns to the hospital. Senturk’s daughter takes the dog home again. She returns to the hospital again. Senturk leaves the hospital after six days. He meets his dog. They are both very happy. Senturk says that a dog can be a best friend. Dogs bring joy . They make people happy. Difficult words: ambulance (a big car that takes sick people to hospital), return (to come back), joy (when somebody feels happy and pleased). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

The debate over the “Zucman tax” in France reflects wider European questions about how much the ultra-rich should contribute. The plan, proposed by economist Gabriel Zucman, calls for a 2% annual levy on fortunes exceeding 100 million euros, affecting approximately 1,800 individuals in France. Supporters argue it would promote tax justice and provide much-needed funds for security, defence, and healthcare. Estimates suggest it could raise 20 billion euros in France and 67 billion euros across the EU. Critics say the figures are unrealistic, warning that the tax may bring far less revenue . They also fear reduced business investment and possible “ tax exile ,” although data shows few wealthy people actually leave their country after tax hikes. Other nations like Spain, Norway, and Switzerland already tax wealth, with mixed results. France itself abolished its wealth tax in 2018, keeping only a real estate tax. The issue continues to spark controversy as governments search for ways to balance budgets. Difficult words: levy (a special tax), justice (when things are fair), revenue (money that a government or company gets), tax exile (when a person or company leaves their country to pay less tax or no tax). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

France is discussing a new “Zucman tax” on very rich people who own more than 100 million euros. Economist Gabriel Zucman wants a 2% tax each year on this group, about 1,800 people in France. Supporters say it is fair because rich people often pay less tax than others, and the money could help hospitals, pensions , and the military. They believe the tax could bring in 20 billion euros in France and even more in the EU. Critics think the number is too high and say rich people may invest less or find ways to avoid paying. Other countries, like Spain, Norway, and Switzerland, already have taxes for very rich people. In France, the old wealth tax ended in 2018, replaced by a tax on property . Difficult words: pension (money for people when they stop working), critic (a person who says what is bad or wrong about something), avoid (to stay away from something or not let it happen), property (houses, lands, or buildings) You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

France talks about a new tax for very rich people. It is a 2% tax on people with more than 100 million euros. About 1,800 people in France would pay this tax. Supporters say that it is fair. It gives more money for schools, hospitals, and the army. They say that the tax can bring 20 billion euros in France and even more in Europe. Critics do not like the idea. They think that rich people may stop investing or try not to pay. Some countries already have a tax like this, for example, Spain, Norway, and Switzerland. In France, the old tax ends in 2018, but people still pay a tax on houses and land. Difficult words: tax (money people must pay to the government), supporter (a person who likes an idea), critic (a person who says what is bad or wrong about something). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Kalundborg, often called “Novo Town,” faces uncertainty as Novo Nordisk, Denmark’s pharmaceutical giant, prepares major job cuts. The company became Europe’s most valuable in 2023 thanks to its weight-loss drug Wegovy; however, competition, slowing sales, and falling share prices have led to restructuring . Novo will cut around 9,000 jobs globally, including 5,000 in Denmark, which has unsettled the local community. Kalundborg hosts a central production hub and employs 5,500 people. The Danish economy remains stronger than much of the euro zone, but the slowdown in pharmaceutical growth has already lowered the central bank’s forecasts. Still, experts argue that Novo’s cutbacks return staffing to 2024 levels after rapid hiring, making the situation manageable. Locals worry about empty houses and job insecurity, while others see advantages: less pressure on housing and more opportunities for other companies to recruit. Despite short-term challenges, many expect Novo to expand again once new factories are complete. Difficult words: restructure (to change how something is organized), unsettle (to make someone feel worried, or unsafe), cutback (a reduction). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

Kalundborg in Denmark is known as “Novo Town” because many people work for Novo Nordisk. The company grew fast with its drug Wegovy, but now sales are slower. Novo wants to cut about 9,000 jobs worldwide, including 5,000 in Denmark. This makes many local people nervous because the town depends on the company. House prices, restaurants, and local shops feel the change. Some people worry about empty houses, while others believe fewer jobs at Novo can help other companies find workers. Experts say the cuts are big but not dangerous for Denmark’s economy . They explain that Novo is only going back to the same number of workers as in 2024. Difficult words: sale (selling something), cut (when something becomes less or fewer), economy (all the money, jobs, and businesses in a country). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Kalundborg is a town in Denmark. Many people there work for a big company, Novo Nordisk. The company makes a lot of money with a drug called Wegovy. Wegovy helps people lose weight . But now the drug sells less, and the company wants to cut many jobs. About 5,000 people will lose their jobs in Denmark. People in the town feel worried about work and houses. Novo still gives a lot of money to Denmark. The economy is strong, but people do not know what will happen next. Some think it will be hard for Kalundborg. Others think it will help because other companies can find more workers. Difficult words: weight (how heavy something is), cut (to make something less or smaller), economy (all the money, jobs, and businesses in a country). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

A new report from the European Court of Auditors reveals that medicine shortages in the European Union have reached record levels in recent years. Between 2022 and October 2024, supplies of 136 critical medicines were insufficient, with 48 critical shortages in 2023 and 46 in 2024. At least 21 of the 27 EU member states were affected, with Belgium, Spain, and France reporting the most serious problems. Amoxicillin, a common antibiotic, and verteporfin, used to treat eye conditions, were among the medicines in short supply. The causes include higher demand, production delays, limited manufacturing capacity, and increased energy costs. Production costs in the EU are estimated to be 20–40% higher than in Asia, leading to heavy reliance on Asian suppliers for raw ingredients and precursors . The situation has significant consequences for patients and national health systems. Reporting rules and stockpiling requirements vary across countries, which makes it difficult to compare shortages or coordinate solutions at the EU level. Difficult words: reliance (when you need something or someone and cannot manage well without it), precursor (a substance from which another is made), coordinate (to organize different parts of work together). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

A report says that the European Union has big problems with medicine shortages . Between 2022 and October 2024, 136 important medicines were missing. In 2023, there were 48 shortages, and in 2024, there were 46. Belgium, Spain, and France had the most serious problems. Many countries also had shortages of antibiotics like amoxicillin. The reasons include high demand , delays in production, not enough capacity , and higher energy prices. Making medicines in the EU is 20–40% more expensive than in Asia, so Europe depends on Asia for most raw materials. The shortages hurt patients and cost national health systems a lot of money. Countries also report shortages in different ways and have different stock rules, which makes it hard to compare the problem. Difficult words: shortage (when there is not enough of something what people need), demand (how much people want or need something), capacity (the amount of something can produce or hold). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

The European Union has many problems with medicines. A report says that 136 important medicines are missing between 2022 and 2024. In 2023, there are 48 shortages , and in 2024, there are 46. Belgium, Spain, and France have the most problems. Amoxicillin, a medicine for infections, is one example. The problem happens because many people need medicines, factories cannot make enough, and energy is expensive. It also costs 20–40% more to make medicines in the EU than in Asia. So the EU often gets materials from Asia. The shortages make life hard for patients and for hospitals. Each country has different rules about reporting and keeping medicines, so it is not easy to know how big the problem is there. Difficult words: missing (not in the place where it should be), shortage (when there is not enough of something what people need), patient (a sick person who is getting medical help). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Disney announced that Jimmy Kimmel Live will return to television after being suspended for six days. The suspension happened after comments Kimmel made about conservative activist Charlie Kirk’s alleged killer created controversy . The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) even threatened to suspend network licenses, which increased political tension. Disney explained it paused the show to avoid inflaming an already emotional moment in the country. The decision sparked a wide political reaction. Many Republicans, including Donald Trump, praised the suspension, claiming Kimmel had low ratings and insulted Kirk. However, democrats and free speech advocates criticized the move, calling it censorship and an attack on freedom of expression. Some politicians, including Republicans like Ted Cruz, defended Kimmel’s right to speak publicly, even if they disagreed with him. After days of discussion with Kimmel, Disney decided to bring the show back, while still noting his comments were insensitive. The debate reminded many Americans that free speech, although protected by law, is fragile and must be defended. Difficult words: suspension (stopping something for a short time), controversy (a situation where people disagree or argue about something), censorship (when the government or another authority blocks or limits speech or media), fragile (easy to break or damage). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

Disney said that Jimmy Kimmel Live will return after one week off the air . The show stopped because Kimmel made comments about Charlie Kirk’s death, and authorities warned ABC about its license . Disney wanted to calm the situation by stopping the program. The decision to stop the show created strong political reactions. Many Republicans, including Trump, were happy, saying Kimmel’s words were bad and his ratings were low. Democrats and free speech groups said it was wrong to stop the show because it limited the right to speak freely. Some politicians, even Republicans, supported Kimmel’s right to talk, even if they didn’t like what he said. After some talks with Kimmel, Disney allowed the show to return, though it also said his comments were not sensitive. Difficult words: off the air (when a TV or radio stops broadcasting something), license (an official permission to do something), rating (a number which shows how many people watch a TV show or listen to a radio program). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Disney says that the show Jimmy Kimmel Live is back on TV. The show stops for six days because Kimmel talks about Charlie Kirk’s death. This makes many people angry. Authorities say ABC can lose its license . Disney stops the show to keep things calm. Some people like the stop. Many Republicans, like Donald Trump, are happy. They say that Kimmel is not funny and says bad things. Other people do not like the stop. They say it is not good for free speech . Everyone should talk in public , even if others do not agree. Disney talks with Kimmel. Then the company says the show can start again. Difficult words: license (an official paper which allows you to do something), free speech (when you can say what you think or believe and nobody can stop you), in public (when you do something where other people can see or hear you). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

President Donald Trump used his UN address to criticise the United Nations and its work sharply, calling climate change a con job and accusing Western countries of going to hell over immigration policy. He joked about a failing teleprompter , then listed his achievements, including his claim to have ended seven un-endable wars early in his term, and complained that the UN didn’t help finalize those deals. Trump attacked what he called empty UN words, criticised international approaches to migration, and warned that uncontrolled flows of people harmed social services and national life. He ridiculed past climate predictions and labeled parts of the green agenda a scam, urging countries to defend citizens and rethink current policies. His speech mixed boasts, warnings, and anecdotes about money and management at the UN complex to underline his point that institutions must produce real results instead of rhetoric. Difficult words: con job (a trick to cheat people and take their money or trust), teleprompter (a machine that shows a speaker their text), finalize (to complete something or make it officially finished), ridicule (to laugh at someone or something in a cruel or unkind way). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

President Trump returned to the UN and criticised the organisation’s effectiveness . He called climate change a con job and warned about migration problems in Western countries. He joked about the teleprompter , then told world leaders he ended seven wars and said the UN didn’t help. Trump said many people crossed borders, and this caused crime and hurt services. He told countries to protect their people and to act against illegal migration. He also said many climate predictions were wrong and called some green policies a scam. In the speech, he spoke about himself, strongly warned about migration, and the role of the United Nations. He said that big organizations only talk but don’t do anything. Difficult words: effectiveness (how well something works or brings the result you want), con job (a trick to make people believe something that is not true to get money or power), teleprompter (a machine which shows a speaker their text), prediction (what you think will happen in the future). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

President Trump speaks at the United Nations. He says the UN does not do a good job. He calls climate change a con . He also says that migration causes big problems for countries. Trump jokes about a teleprompter which does not work. Then talks about ending wars. He says that he ends seven wars without help from other countries. He says that many people come to Europe. This hurts services and causes crime. He asks countries to keep their people safe and check their borders. He also says that some climate ideas are not real and hurt countries. Trump speaks about himself a lot. He warns other leaders, too. Difficult words: con (a trick to cheat someone), teleprompter (a machine which shows a speaker their words), service (help or work for someone, a system of help for people). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

The Duchess of York, Sarah Ferguson, has been removed as patron of Julia’s House, a UK children’s hospice charity, after an email surfaced in which she called convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein her supreme friend. The email, revealed by newspapers, dates back to 2011, after Epstein had already been convicted. While Ferguson had publicly distanced herself from him, in private she apologized and praised him as loyal and generous. Her spokesperson later said she wrote the message to avoid legal problems. The charity said it would be inappropriate for Ferguson to continue supporting their work with very ill children. Ferguson had been involved since 2018, joining other well-known figures connected to the charity. A spokesperson for the Duchess said she wouldn’t comment on the decision. Other charities, including Teenage Cancer Trust and youth organizations, are now reviewing their ties with her. The case raises questions about reputation , responsibility, and how charities manage their public image. Difficult words: patron (a famous or important person who supports a group, often a charity), hospice (a place that cares for very sick people who may not get better), distance (to move away from someone or something), reputation (what people think about someone). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

Sarah Ferguson, the Duchess of York, lost her role as patron of Julia’s House, a UK charity for sick children. The charity said it is not right for her to continue after an email showed she called Jeffrey Epstein her good friend. The email was from 2011. In public, she said being close to Epstein was a big mistake, but she wrote kind words to him. Her team later explained she only did this to stop possible legal trouble. Epstein was a sex offende r, and the charity wanted to protect its work and name. Ferguson became a patron in 2018, but now her connection ended. She didn’t comment on the case. Other charities, like Teenage Cancer Trust, are checking if they will also keep her as a patron. Difficult words: patron (a famous or important person who supports a group, often a charity), sex offender (a person who does a sexual offense), connection (a link or relationship between people or things). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Sarah Ferguson is the Duchess of York. She is not a patron of Julia’s House anymore. Julia’s House is a UK charity for very sick children. The charity says that she cannot stay because she calls Jeffrey Epstein her friend in an email. The email is from 2011. Epstein is a man who does bad crimes in the past. In public , Ferguson says that it is bad to be Epstein’s friend. But then, she writes an email to him with nice words. Ferguson starts with the charity in 2018. The charity thanks her for her help. Other charities now look if they want her to stay or not. Difficult words: charity (a group which helps people who need money or things to live a better life), in public (in front of other people). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

A Belgian company named PermaFungi is transforming used coffee grounds into edible mushrooms and insulation tiles. At a former industrial site in Brussels, workers harvest oyster mushrooms that grow mainly on coffee grounds and straw. The straw stops the mushrooms from growing on urban waste. The company collects 5.5 tons of coffee waste every month from cafes across the country. Workers mix the coffee grounds in a large drum, they add the mushroom parts, and then they transfer the mixture to small bags. After 15 days, they harvest the mushrooms. PermaFungi uses the residue from their oyster mushroom farms to create a biodegradable material that can replace plastic. They add mycelium . The company says that their method of growing mushrooms could dramatically reduce urban waste. Governments around the world prioritize the idea of the circular economy , and mycelium insulation tiles could be a solution. Difficult words: residue (something that remains after the main part is taken or used), mycelium (the root-like structure of a mushroom), circular economy (a system that intends to limit consumption and waste). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

A Belgian company uses coffee grounds to grow mushrooms and to make insulation tiles. Every month, the company collects 5.5 tons of coffee grounds, which are usually waste. Workers mix the grounds with mushroom spores , and they put this mixture in small bags. The mushrooms take 15 days to grow. After they collect the mushrooms, workers use the remains to make a material which could replace plastic. The company makes insulation tiles, and it hopes to make 13 tons of the material a month by 2025. It could help solve problem with too much waste. Difficult words: coffee grounds (the remains after you make coffee), insulation (protection from heat, sound, electricity, and other things), spore (a very small part of a plant or mushroom from which a new plant or mushroom grows). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

A Belgian company grows mushrooms from coffee grounds. Coffee grounds are leftover coffee. You have them after you make coffee. They are usually waste. The company gets 5.5 tons of coffee grounds from cafes every month. Workers mix the grounds with mushrooms spores . Then the mushrooms grow inside small bags. Mushrooms need 15 days to grow. Workers then harvest the mushrooms. They empty the bags. They use the material to make insulation tiles. Insulation tiles protect a place. By 2025, the company plans to make 13 tons of tiles every month. The plan is a good way to use less plastic. Difficult words: waste (materials and things which people throw away), spore (a very small part of a plant or mushroom from which a new plant or mushroom grows), harvest (to pick fruit or plants to eat). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Several major European airports, including Heathrow, Brussels, and Berlin, faced major disruption after a cyber-attack damaged the electronic check-in and baggage system used by many airlines. Collins Aerospace, the company responsible for the software, was directly affected, leading to long delays, flight cancellations, and confusion for travelers. At Brussels Airport, passengers were advised not to arrive unless their flight was confirmed, while Berlin reported long waiting times. Heathrow mainly struggled with severe delays, which created a chain of missed connections across Europe. Travel experts explained that the incident happened on a busy summer travel day, which increased its impact. Airlines now need to rebook passengers, provide meals, and arrange accommodation when delays are very long. However, travelers cannot expect financial compensation , since the airlines were not at fault. The cyber-attack highlights the vulnerability of aviation systems and shows how quickly a technical problem can cause large-scale disruption, with tens of thousands of passengers affected in just one day. Difficult words: disruption (a problem that stops something working normally), compensation (money you get when something goes wrong), vulnerability (weakness that can be attacked). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

Heathrow Airport in London had problems because of a cyber-attack on check-in and baggage software. Brussels and Berlin airports also had big delays. The problem started with Collins Aerospace, the company that makes the system. In Brussels, many flights stopped, and passengers had to wait for a long time. Berlin also had long lines. Heathrow had many delays, which made people miss connections to other flights. Travel reporters said the attack was serious because it happened on a busy travel day. Airlines now need to give passengers new flights, food, and hotels when delays are too long. But travelers won’t get money, because the airlines didn’t cause the problem. The attack shows how one system problem can hurt travel across many airports in Europe. Difficult words: cyber-attack (an online attack on computers), baggage (suitcases and bags), connection (the link between two flights). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Heathrow Airport in London has a big problem. A cyber-attack hits the computer for check-in and bags. Brussels and Berlin airports also have problems. People wait for a long time. Some flights stop. In Brussels, people wait for many hours, and some flights stop. In Berlin, people stand in long lines. At Heathrow, many flights are late. People cannot take the next flight when the first flight is late. Collins Aerospace is the company with the problem. This company makes the computer system at airports. Airlines give food, a hotel, and new flights to people. But airlines do not give money, because it is not their mistake . The cyber-attack makes airports in Europe very slow. The attack shows that one problem has an impact on thousands of people. Difficult words: flight (when a plane flies), airline (a company which operates planes), mistake (when you do something wrong). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

Web3 is a decentralized Internet. Instead of a few technology companies running the Internet, it will use blockchain technology. Many computers control blockchains instead of one company. In Paris, nine decapitated pig heads appeared outside several mosques, sparking concern over Islamophobia and national unrest. Authorities suspect Russia may be involved in previous similar incidents, which targeted Jewish sites and a Holocaust memorial. Recent cases involved Serbian and Bulgarian nationals, sometimes orchestrated by Russian actors, according to French security services. However, Moscow denies involvement. Such operations aim to destabilize France and inflame social tensions. France continues to investigate these incidents to protect national security. In the US, it has spread far beyond its traditional base in the Northeast, reaching states like California and Florida. While there are 48 million fans worldwide, TV audiences are modest. Experts say that despite Olympic exposure , mainstream success could take decades. Difficult words: elite (a group seen as superior compared to the rest of society), net worth (the difference between total assets and liabilities, showing the overall wealth of a person or company), exposure (public attention or visibility).
